The phase-field model is used to investigate the evolution of the entire directional solidification process.
The thermal gradient G is constant at 100 K/mm, while the pulling speed Vp increases from 0 to 300 μm/s over 0.5 s.
The evolution of solute concentration c0 and interface velocity VI shows dissipative features, including peaks, oscillations, and a final steady state.
Smaller diffusion coefficient D corresponds to higher dissipation, leading to more interfaces forming during solidification.
The planar instability is triggered by the decrease in interfacial energy due to solute segregation, rather than the interface velocity.
During the planar-to-cellular transition, smaller D leads to longer transition time, higher peak c0, lower VI, and larger cellular wavelength.
In the dendrite growth stage, smaller D results in more side-branches, even with the same primary arm spacing and tip velocity.
At the steady-state stage, smaller D leads to lower c0 at the interface, smaller tip curvature, and fewer/smaller side-branches.
The ratio τ/W^2, which determines the competitive influences of curvature and velocity, is dominated by the diffusion coefficient D and the degree of dissipation.

Different initial conditions can lead to quite different solidification morphologies, even with the same solidification parameters, demonstrating the history-dependent nature of the dissipative solidification process.
The phase-field simulations show good consistency with theoretical predictions, especially for the planar instability onset.
The domain size of the phase-field simulations is 2400 x 2400 grids, corresponding to 288.0 μm x 288.0 μm in real units.
It takes about 30 hours using 40 cores to finish one phase-field simulation job.
The paper provides new perspectives on solidification evolution by investigating the entire process from the viewpoint of dissipative dynamics.
The investigations on the effect of diffusion coefficient can provide theoretical bases for parameter optimization and material design in engineering applications.
